title: Automatic retirement saving expands retirement and liquid-account ownership while also increasing short-term credit-card debt
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35373 SIPP comparison of Oregon Auto-IRA exposure with similar private-sector workers in not-yet-adopting states, as summarized by the Georgetown Center for Retirement Initiatives
geography: United States; Oregon policy exposure compared with workers in not-yet-adopting states

observations.period: Oregon Auto-IRA rollout; study period and SIPP comparison described in 2026 working paper

denominator.unit: private-sector workers likely exposed to OregonSaves compared with similar workers in not-yet-adopting states; exact analytic counts are not disclosed in the public summary

ira_balance_change.unit: more than US dollars in reported IRA balances

observations.method: Published summary of NBER Working Paper 35373 using SIPP data and a comparison of Oregon private-sector workers likely exposed to OregonSaves with similar workers in states that had not yet adopted an Auto-IRA; the paper uses policy exposure and firm-size rollout timing rather than a simple before/after count.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not disclose full analytic sample counts, event-study specification, confidence intervals, contribution rates, withdrawals, cash-outs, take-home-pay effects, or subgroup estimates. The source is a 2026 working paper and the numerical details here are reported through a secondary policy summary.
observations.subgroup: Private-sector workers likely exposed to OregonSaves and comparison workers in not-yet-adopting states; exact subgroup cells are not available in the public summary.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher retirement balances can represent real long-term asset accumulation without proving improved current liquidity, and the balance change may reflect contributions, employer plans, market movement, or other composition differences.

observations.period: Oregon Auto-IRA rollout; household liquidity and credit-card outcomes

denominator.unit: same study-specific worker comparison; exact analytic counts and item universes are not disclosed in the public summary

observations.method: Secondary summary of the NBER SIPP quasi-experimental comparison; checking/savings outcomes and credit-card debt are interpreted alongside retirement-account outcomes rather than as a single net-security index.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not show debt interest rates, minimum payments, credit limits, utilization, delinquency, withdrawals, cash-outs, consumption, or whether the debt was temporary. It also does not establish that the policy caused a welfare loss or that the added debt was harmful.
observations.subgroup: Study-specific exposed and comparison private-sector workers; no public subgroup estimates promoted.
observations.counterinterpretation: Short-term borrowing can coexist with larger liquid or retirement assets and may reflect a household smoothing contributions or managing a newly opened account; conversely, debt can carry fees and interest that reduce usable household room.

related_sources.claim: Primary NBER working-paper abstract and study design: SIPP comparison of Oregon Auto-IRA exposure with similar workers in not-yet-adopting states.
Georgetown Center for Retirement Initiatives summary reporting the numerical balance-sheet effects.

boundary: This record shows that automatic retirement saving can move several balance-sheet margins at once: retirement ownership/assets, checking/savings ownership/balances, and credit-card debt. It does not establish a single net welfare effect, take-home-pay change, consumption response, debt cost, contribution/withdrawal mechanism, retirement adequacy, or effects by income, age, race, or job type. The public summary should not be treated as a substitute for the full NBER paper or a new independent SIPP estimate.
